titulo: The wall behind the pharmacy counter
subtitulo: Describe the pain, learn what needs a prescription, and escalate cleanly if it becomes a real emergency
cena: The pharmacist's hand is already reaching toward two different shelves, and only one of them is going to require a document you don't have.
frasePiso: The only defensive part of this module: name the pain, learn the rule before you argue with it, and know the one number that ends the guessing.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: Mexico's national emergency number is 911, covering ambulance, police and fire; in Mexico City the Red Cross ambulance service can also be reached directly at 065.
fatosDatados.fonte: Servicio de emergencias 911 (nacional); Cruz Roja Mexicana

fatosDatados.afirmacao: Since a 2010 COFEPRIS rule, Mexican pharmacies may not sell antibiotics without a prescription issued by a physician licensed in Mexico; a prescription from another country is not accepted at the counter.
fatosDatados.fonte: COFEPRIS — regulamento de venda de antibióticos (2010)

steps.pt: The one openly defensive part of the module — mostly small, a headache, a question. But these four moves scale to a real emergency.
My head hurts.

steps.promptPt: At the pharmacy counter, name the pain before asking for anything. Speak now.
steps.pt: My head hurts.
Since when does it hurt?
Duration is the first thing a pharmacist needs, not a diagnosis — keep it to one clean answer.
Since yesterday.

steps.promptPt: The pharmacist asks since when. Answer with one clean phrase: since yesterday. Speak now.
steps.pt: Since yesterday.

steps.es: Le recomiendo este para el dolor.
steps.pt: I recommend this one for the pain.
steps.tts: Le recomiendo este para el dolor.

steps.pt: Since 2010, pharmacies can't sell antibiotics without a Mexico-licensed prescription — a foreign one won't work here either. Ask first.
Do I need a prescription for this medication?

steps.promptPt: Before you take anything to the till, ask whether this medication needs a prescription. Speak now.
steps.pt: Do I need a prescription for this medication?
No, this one doesn't need a prescription.
One more filter, connecting to B13 — the allergy sentence applies at the pharmacy counter too.

steps.es: Tengo una alergia. ¿Tiene algo sin aspirina?
steps.pinyin: TEN-goh OO-nah ah-LEHR-hyah. TYEH-neh AHL-goh seen ahs-pee-REE-nah
steps.pt: I have an allergy. Do you have something without aspirin?
steps.tts: Tengo una alergia. ¿Tiene algo sin aspirina?

steps.promptPt: You cannot take aspirin. Say so and ask for an alternative. Speak now.
steps.es: Tengo una alergia. ¿Tiene algo sin aspirina?
steps.pinyin: TEN-goh OO-nah ah-LEHR-hyah. TYEH-neh AHL-goh seen ahs-pee-REE-nah
steps.pt: I have an allergy. Do you have something without aspirin?
Yes, this one is with paracetamol.
Now the scale-up — same four moves, but the object is a real emergency and the phone is the counter.
911, what is your emergency?

steps.promptPt: Someone next to you has collapsed. Call and say you need an ambulance. Speak now.
steps.pt: I need an ambulance.
What is your location?
911 covers the whole country — ambulance, police, fire, one number. Give the address you made portable in B04.

steps.promptPt: Give your location using the hotel name and room number. Speak now.
steps.es: Estoy en el hotel, en la habitación trescientos cinco.
steps.pinyin: ehs-TOY en el oh-TEL, en lah ah-bee-tah-SYOHN trehs-SYEHN-tohs SEEN-koh
steps.pt: I'm at the hotel, in room three hundred five.
steps.tts: Estoy en el hotel, en la habitación trescientos cinco.

steps.pt: We're on our way.

steps.promptPt: New symptom, same frame. Speak now.
steps.pt: Do you have something for a sore throat?

steps.promptPt: They said the first one needs one. Ask for the alternative. Speak now.
steps.pt: Is there something without a prescription?

steps.promptPt: You bought it. Now find out the dose. Speak now.
steps.pinyin: meh PWEH-deh eks-plee-KAHR KOH-moh seh TOH-mah
steps.pt: Can you explain how to take it?

steps.promptPt: Simplest version of the whole exchange. Speak now.
steps.pinyin: meh dah AHL-goh PAH-rah el doh-LOHR
steps.pt: Can I have something for the pain?

steps.es: Me duele la cabeza. ¿Necesito receta para este medicamento? Necesito una ambulancia.
steps.pinyin: meh DWEH-leh lah kah-BEH-sah. neh-seh-SEE-toh reh-SEH-tah PAH-rah EHS-teh meh-dee-kah-MEHN-toh. neh-seh-SEE-toh OO-nah ahm-boo-LAHN-syah
steps.pt: Shadow the small version and the scaled-up version of the same four moves.
steps.tts: Me duele la cabeza. ¿Necesito receta para este medicamento? Necesito una ambulancia.

steps.pt: B17 complete. Name it, timeframe, ask the constraint — receta, alergia. If it scales up: 911, ambulance, the address.

aprofundar.titulo: The counter has a rule the traveller cannot see

secoes.titulo: The prescription wall is not personal
secoes.corpo: Since 2010, COFEPRIS has required a valid prescription from a Mexico-licensed physician for antibiotics. A foreign prescription, however official, is not accepted at the counter. Ask ¿necesita receta? before assuming a familiar medicine will be sold over the counter.

secoes.titulo: 911 is the one number, for everything
secoes.corpo: Unlike some countries that split police, fire and ambulance into different numbers, Mexico's national emergency line is 911 for all three. In Mexico City, Cruz Roja's own ambulance line, 065, is a parallel option, not a replacement.
A pharmacist's first useful question is almost always about time, not cause. Desde ayer, desde esta mañana — a one-line duration answer keeps the exchange moving toward a recommendation.

secoes.titulo: Allergy does not stop applying at the pharmacy
secoes.corpo: The B13 discipline — name the allergen plainly — is exactly as valid over the counter as it is in a kitchen. Tengo una alergia works in both places without modification.

permissao: You are allowed to ask the boring bureaucratic question before the useful one. Asking ¿necesito receta? before you've even said what's wrong is not paranoid — it's the fastest way to find out whether this counter can actually help you.
espelho: Anyone who has ever been told 'you need a doctor's note for that' at a pharmacy back home already knows this exact wall exists everywhere in some form — Mexico's version is stricter about antibiotics specifically, but the underlying experience of a rule the counter can't bend is not foreign at all.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You ask for a common antibiotic you'd normally buy without a prescription at home, and the pharmacist says no and won't budge, even when you explain it's routine where you're from.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: This pharmacist is being unusually strict, or there's a way around it if I explain myself better.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: This isn't the pharmacist's personal judgment call — Mexican federal regulation has required a prescription for antibiotics since 2010, and pharmacists who sell without one risk real regulatory consequences, so there is no version of this conversation that ends in a sale.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Ask ¿necesita receta? before you commit to wanting a specific medication, and if the answer is yes, ask what a local clinic near here can do instead.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You stop spending time on a request that was never going to be granted and move straight to the option that actually works — a nearby clinic or doctor.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not for the wide range of medications that don't require a prescription in Mexico — many common pain relievers and over-the-counter remedies are sold freely; the rule is specifically about antibiotics.
